The CRTC Is Officially Actively Reviewing CBC's GamerGate Coverage: The Uphill Battle Begins Now!

After seven months of waiting, the CRTC's investigation of the CBC concerning its biased reporting on GamerGate finally reached active review status as of yesterday morning. Unfortunately, the clear and definitive victory we were hoping for failed to materialize, but this particular battle is still far from over.

First, the bad news: The CRTC believes that the CBC's coverage of GamerGate in its November 13, 2014 hit piece - where our consumer revolt was described as "initially (being) a social media hashtag for discussion of ethics in gaming journalism, (which) has increasingly become a catch phrase for the online harassment of female gamers" - was an acceptable summary of our history.

Staff recognizes that Gamer Gate is not a concerted, centralized effort by a single group, but rather a complicated issue with many loosely affiliated groups each perceiving it to mean something very specific that may, or may not, be compatible with what other groups believe it to be. Staff further recognizes that, as stated in your complaint, Gamer Gate stands for some as a banner under which individuals gather to question ethics in gaming journalism, but notes that it is also perceived by others, as noted in the CBC segment, as "a catch phrase for the online harassment of female gamers."

Now, the silver lining here is that the CRTC - which is part of a department of the Government of Canada - has at least acknowledged that not only does the "ethics in gaming journalism" aspect of GamerGate exist, but also that it came first.

Further, the reporter took the time to briefly present the two main sides of Gamer Gate, although she did so in a chronological manner, which you may not think reflects the situation as it is.

Now, I realize many of you are disheartened by this, but don't throw up your hands and give up just yet. We're still in the race for a few reasons.

The first bit of good news is that the CRTC has started asking the CBC questions concerning the lack of visibility of the CBC Ombudsman's reviews of complaints we've filed.

However, Commission staff notes that in the Complaints section of the CBC’s Journalistic Standards and Practices it is noted that:

"If the complainant is not satisfied with the explanations given and applies to the Ombudsman for a review, CBC undertakes to make the Ombudsman’s opinion accessible by, among other means, posting a link on the program web page or on the page giving access to the content in question." (emphasis ours)

Staff therefore asks the CBC Ombudsman’s office to clarify what action(s) it has undertaken to make the Ombudsman’s opinion on this matter accessible to viewers of this segment on their website.

The second bit of good news - which I personally verified with our caseworker today - is that the review has apparently not been finalized and I can still submit evidence or questions to the CRTC commission for them to take into consideration. What's great about this is that the hit piece at the center of this review is actually our strongest case against the CBC, as it can be conclusively proven that the interviewee whose claims of harassment they touted as representative of GamerGate's behavior was almost completely fabricated and the fact that she made significant lies of omission is something that I can prove beyond a reasonable doubt:

http://lunararchivist.tumblr.com/post/109644115186/gamergate-media-watch-part-2-gamerella-girl

The last piece of good news is that I'm preparing to file a second complaint with the CRTC about the CBC's coverage of GamerGate and that this one will cover all the batshit crazy things they've done since February 2015, such as using the Law & Order: Special Victims Unit episode to frame a debate about GamerGate, one of their radio hosts comparing one of us to a Holocaust denier, and another saying that we threatened to rape and murder female game developers. Right now, I'm waiting for our caseworker to get back to me on a few things before submission and am using the time to recharge my batteries and assemble a more solid case. To this end, I've been trying to preemptively secure help from our stable of pro-GamerGate writers and journalists - such as Milo Yiannopoulos, Allum Bokhari, William Usher, Ashe Schow, /u/Calbeck, etc. - to make sure our argument's as airtight as we can possibly make it.

As always, I'll keep you guys updated on any further developments.

Linux Mint (XFCE if you have old hardware) seems to be the linux of choice for windows refugees.

It is interesting that windows users expect Linux to run their games. Do People switching from Mac(or other OSs) to windows expect windows to run their Mac games, their Amiga games, their Atari games?

Honestly, I would use XFCE anyway. It looks the most like winXP, is quite lightweight, which is good if you you are doing a lot of CPU or GPU intensive tasks, and, in my experience, runs smoother than KDE/Gnome3x/Unity. It's all a DE needs to be without needing hoity toity compositing.
I tend to prefer LXDE for my lightweight systems, but XFCE is a good choice as well for sure.
I think I went XFCE over LXDE because of dual monitor wallpaper/screen saver options. They both pretty much looked about the same, although IIRC XFCE came in with less system overhead.

If you want to learn linux, I'd start by just using something easy to set up and maintain like Linux Mint for your everyday work for a while, and then start looking into command-line stuff. I rather like these resources for that command line:

http://linuxcommand.org/tlcl.php http://conqueringthecommandline.com/book

If you want to play vidya games, I recommend keeping your windows install for that. Games don't run that well in virtual machines. Native gaming on Linux has been steadily improving (especially with the introduction of steam), but it just ain't there yet. I find I can usually get stuff running with WINE (a windows emulator), but it often takes a lot of time and effort. I've personally decided it's easier just to have a windows install lying around.

Honestly? Installing an operating system is like installing any other program through a wizard. The difference being that you have an extra step to go through with partitioning if you want to dual boot (keep Windows and choose which OS to boot into when you turn on your PC). Look at the guides, but also, if you're a visual learner like me, look at a Youtube video as well of someone walking through how to install [operating system here]. Just make sure it's a fairly recent video.

TBH, just drop in a Ubuntu (or derivative, I use xubuntu, but I hear good things about mint) disc and go from there. It works better out of the box than vanilla windows, handles updates better, installs programs better, and neater, than windows, and is more stable than any MS OS. For gaming, if it isn't native, on which they have made fantastic headway of late, then just install wine and google "how to install wine|playonlinux on $DISTRO" where $DISTRO is your linux distribution of choice. Honestly, I use xubuntu because I used XP for most of my life, and it was like slipping on an old shoe, all I had to do was re-lace it.

If you have drive space and don't want to do a dual boot just yet you can use linux with Oracle VM VirtualBox. It's free to use and easy to setup. You install VirtualBox and download the version of linux you want to use. Then create the VM (instructions) and let it install... fairly easy. Then if you like it and everything works well then you can do the dual boot or just use linux by itself.
I have tried most of the "user friendly" distros and really like Elementary fwiw

Linux is the catch-all name for a series of operating systems that are based on the Linux Kernel/Core.

Linux operating systems are heavily tied to the console/terminal for using and configuring many components. However, fear not, there are many Graphical User Interfaces (GUI) for 99% of the stuff you will actually use linux for. In fact, you could spend years never touching the console/command line.

How does this compare to windows you may ask?

Windows started very much like Linux, heavily command line based. If you're curious as to what its like look around for "CMD" and "PowerShell." Windows (I suppose after 3.1) heavily invested in creating applications with GUI which is much easier for your average user to use.

Windows also invested early in end user products and created suites of business ready applications that encouraged it's adoption. Users got used to using it for their job and so they adopted it for their home.

Today both operating systems are miles ahead of where they were 20 years ago and both can be used for nearly any/all your application needs. If 99% of what you do is surf the web, watch netflix and edit text documents either is fine.
PowerShell is just a toy compared to a Linux shell (any one of them). The Linux shell is a source of power and magic. Case in point.
The Ubuntu community is very newbie friendly and helpful and is a great resource for someone starting out with Linux. That's why I think it's such a great starter distro.
If you play a lot of games you really should check to see if the ones you play the most will run on linux. Linux has support for a lot of games, but, there's still ones that don't work yet.

Fire up gnome terminal and get familiar with the SHELL. It has thousands of programs that may be strung together in an input output fashion.

Long story short, it will turn you into a god capable of doing more work that 1000 lackies chained to their cubicles could accomplish in 1000 years. It will allow your reach to extend across the globe, and make the electric eye work for you.

If you have a second computer you can use, I suggest starting to experiment with that one before you dual-boot on your main computer.

When you start to switch OS and still have stuff on both so you have to dual-boot often, it becomes annoying very fast.

Get a Linux Mint 17.2 iso file and make a live bootable USB or DVD. Boot off of it. Mess around with it, nothing bad will happen. Get to know it. Finally, when you're confident enough, install it. Love it. Own it. Be it.

Playing games is one of the things that Linux just doesn't do as well as Windows right now (market forces really) but you're on the right path wanting to use virtual machines https://teksyndicate.com/videos/gta-v-linux-skylake-build-hardware-vm-passthrough

VM passthrough is where you basically pass though near complete access of hardware to the virtual machine, basically your virtual machine will be able to use your graphics card for gaming in a Windows virtual machine. The host of that video I've linked is using Arch Linux (not noob friendly) but you can grab the equivalent or alternative software for whatever copy of Linux you go for (I'd recommend a Ubuntu variant).
